titulo: Overtourism: when cities start to push visitors away

fuente.nota: Written for the language panel. The figures are approximate and should not be cited as a source.

parrafos: It is not yet nine in the morning, but the narrow street leading to the cathedral is already full. Groups follow guides holding up umbrellas and small flags; cruise passengers, wearing identical stickers, stop every few metres to take photographs; a delivery van tries in vain to get through. A woman carrying her shopping squeezes past, sighs and disappears into a doorway. She is one of the few residents left in a street where, only a decade ago, almost every flat was a family home.

Scenes like this have become familiar in dozens of European cities, from Venice to Dubrovnik, from Amsterdam to the old centres of Barcelona, Lisbon and Seville. After the eerie silence of the pandemic, travel has returned with remarkable force, and international arrivals in Europe have climbed back above their previous records. For national economies, this is welcome news. For many of the people who live in the most visited neighbourhoods, however, it is starting to feel like an invasion. Cheap flights, giant cruise ships and social media, which sends thousands of people to the same photogenic corners, have all played their part.

The word that sums up their frustration is 'overtourism': the point at which the number of visitors damages the quality of life of residents and, sometimes, the experience of the visitors themselves. It is not simply a question of numbers. A city can welcome millions of tourists a year without serious problems if they are spread out in time and space. The trouble starts when crowds concentrate in the same few streets, at the same hours, during the same months of the year. Then rubbish piles up, public transport is overwhelmed and even a simple walk to the bakery becomes an obstacle course.

Housing lies at the heart of the conflict. In historic districts, a growing share of flats has been converted into short-term holiday rentals, which are far more profitable for owners than long-term leases. Local shops selling bread or hardware give way to souvenir stores, ice-cream parlours and luggage lockers. Neighbours complain of noise at night and of suitcases rattling over the cobblestones at dawn. 'It is not that we hate tourists,' says a retired teacher in a southern Spanish city. 'It is that there is no neighbourhood left.'

In recent summers, that discontent has spilled onto the streets. Residents' associations in several Spanish cities, as well as in the Balearic and Canary Islands, have organised marches under slogans calling for a different model of tourism. In one widely reported protest, demonstrators sprayed visitors sitting at restaurant terraces with water pistols, a gesture that was more symbolic than aggressive but made headlines around the world. Similar protests, smaller but no less angry, have taken place in Italy, Portugal and Greece.

Local authorities have begun to react, each in its own way. Venice now charges day-trippers an entry fee on the busiest days, an experiment watched closely by other cities. Amsterdam has blocked the construction of new hotels, restricted guided tours in its red-light district and launched campaigns telling certain kinds of visitors to stay away. Barcelona has promised to phase out licences for tourist flats over the coming years, while several cities have raised their tourist taxes or limited the number of cruise ships allowed to dock.

Not everyone is convinced. Hoteliers, restaurant owners and shopkeepers point out that tourism supports millions of jobs and accounts for more than a tenth of the economy in countries such as Spain, Italy and Greece. Restrictions, they warn, could push visitors towards rival destinations and hurt workers who are already poorly paid. Some economists add that entry fees and higher taxes may simply turn city centres into theme parks that only the wealthy can afford, without solving the underlying problem. Tourists, after all, still need to sleep, eat and move around somewhere.

Others argue that the real issue is not how many tourists come, but how the benefits and costs are shared out. The income from tourism often goes to hotel chains, online platforms and property owners, while the costs, from cleaning the streets to rising rents, fall on residents and local councils. Tourist taxes, if they are used to improve public services and housing for locals, could help to correct that imbalance. So could policies that encourage visitors to travel outside the peak season or to explore less famous areas.

Technology may also lend a hand. Some cities are experimenting with real-time data from mobile phones to measure crowding and redirect visitors towards quieter spots, or with compulsory booking systems for the most popular monuments. Others are trying to attract a different type of traveller, one who stays longer, spends more in local businesses and comes outside the summer months. Whether such strategies can work on a large scale is still uncertain, but they reflect a clear shift in thinking.

For decades, the success of a tourist destination was measured by a single figure: how many visitors it attracted each year. That logic is now being questioned. As evening falls on the cathedral street, the groups have gone, and the woman with the shopping bags reappears on her balcony. The street is quiet for a few hours. Tomorrow, she knows, the crowds will be back. The question facing Europe's most beautiful cities is whether they can remain places to live in, and not only places to visit.
titulo_es: Mass tourism: when cities start pushing visitors away
resumen_es: Report on tourist overcrowding in European cities: its effects on housing and on residents' lives, the protests, the measures taken by the authorities (taxes, caps, licences) and the debate on how to share benefits and costs.

ideas_clave.idea: Driven by cheap flights, cruises and social media, tourism has returned to record levels since the pandemic, and residents of the busiest historic centres feel overwhelmed.
Overtourism occurs when visitors are so concentrated in space and time that they harm residents' quality of life, not just when their total number is high.
The conversion of homes into holiday rentals and the replacement of everyday shops are driving residents out of historic districts.
This anger has led to street protests in Spain and other southern European countries.
Cities such as Venice, Amsterdam and Barcelona have introduced entry fees, limits on hotels and tourist flats, higher taxes and restrictions on cruise ships.
The tourism industry and some economists warn that restrictions could cost jobs and make cities exclusive without fixing the problem.
An alternative approach focuses on sharing the gains more fairly, spreading visitors over time and space, and using data and booking systems.
Cities are moving away from measuring success by visitor numbers and must ensure they remain places where people can live.

resumen_modelo: The text describes the growing tension between tourism and residents in Europe's most visited cities. After the pandemic, visitor numbers have reached new records, and in historic centres such as those of Venice, Barcelona or Lisbon local people increasingly feel invaded. The problem, known as overtourism, arises less from the total number of tourists than from their concentration in the same places and periods. Its most visible consequence concerns housing: flats are turned into holiday rentals and traditional shops disappear, pushing residents out. This frustration has led to protests in Spain and other Mediterranean countries. In response, authorities have adopted various measures, including entry fees, limits on hotels and tourist flats, higher taxes and fewer cruise ships. The industry, however, warns that such restrictions threaten jobs in economies that depend heavily on tourism and could make cities accessible only to the rich. Others believe the key is to distribute the benefits more fairly, to spread visitors more evenly and to use technology to manage flows. The article concludes that cities must stop judging success by visitor numbers alone and remain places to live.
